We prove that the resulting projected adjoint process satisfies a discrete-time Pontryagin principle and converges, as the time step tends to zero, to the solution of the corresponding continuous-time adjoint backward stochastic differential equation. Numerical experiments illustrate the accuracy, stability, and scalability of the approach.

Optimization and Control.title: Matching Lower Bounds for Randomized First-Order Methods in Hessian-Lipschitz Nonconvex Optimization
Optimization and Control.summary: We establish a randomized first-order lower bound for finding an $ε$-stationary point, $\|\nabla f(x)\|\le ε$, of a nonconvex function with initial gap at most $Δ$, $L_1$-Lipschitz gradient, and $L_2$-Lipschitz Hessian. Each oracle call returns the exact function value and gradient. Let $Q_{\mathrm{rand},\mathrm{FO}}^{\infty}(ε;Δ,L_1,L_2)$ denote the minimax number of calls, maximized over finite dimensions, for arbitrary adaptive randomized algorithms with per-instance success probability at least $2/3$. In the regime $ε\lesssim L_1^2/L_2$ and $ΔL_2^{1/2}ε^{-3/2}\gtrsim 1$, we prove $ Q_{\mathrm{rand},\mathrm{FO}}^{\infty}(ε;Δ,L_1,L_2) \ge c\,ΔL_1^{1/2}L_2^{1/4}ε^{-7/4}, $ where $c>0$ is an absolute constant. This matches the deterministic restarted accelerated-gradient upper bound of Li and Lin (2023) and extends the sharp deterministic lower bound of Zhou (2026) to unrestricted randomized algorithms. Thus, randomization does not improve the high-dimensional worst-case query rate. The construction keeps quadratic curvature visible while revealing the forcing directions sequentially. Large eigenspaces limit preprocessing, and a scheduled-disclosure coupling makes each fresh direction incur a separate cost.

Optimization and Control.title: Matching Randomized First-Order Bounds for Higher-Order Smooth Nonconvex Optimization
Optimization and Control.summary: Does randomization improve the worst-case first-order complexity of nonconvex optimization when the objective is very smooth? We prove that, for every fixed finite integer $p\ge3$, finding an $\eps$-stationary point requires $Ω_p(\eps^{-5/3})$ exact value-and-gradient queries, even for $C^\infty$ objectives with initial gap at most one and simultaneous global Lipschitz budgets of one for derivatives of orders $1,\ldots,p$. Together with the known deterministic upper bound, this determines the accuracy exponent up to a single logarithmic factor. The lower bound holds for unrestricted adaptive randomized algorithms, unbounded query locations, and outputs that need not have been queried. One algorithm-independent hard distribution suffices in dimension $O_p(\eps^{-47/3})$. The construction combines a block-chain potential with an exact quartic core, repeated quadratic spectra, and two static Gaussian tensor perturbations. A scheduled Haar argument controls the entire adaptive query span. An innovation-only Gaussian comparison then bounds exact transcript information without assuming finite precision or a minimum query separation. This establishes the $5/3$ randomized accuracy barrier under every prescribed finite smoothness order, extending the previously matched third-order case.

Optimization and Control.title: Sharp Fresh-Gradient Complexity of Nonconvex-Strongly-Concave Minimax Optimization
Optimization and Control.summary: We characterize the fresh-gradient oracle complexity of smooth nonconvex-strongly-concave minimax optimization, with matching upper and lower bounds up to logarithmic factors. Let $Φ(x)=\max_y f(x,y)$, where $f$ is jointly $L$-smooth and $μ$-strongly concave in $y$ on unconstrained Euclidean domains, and set $κ=L/μ$. Each query returns a fresh unbiased joint gradient with conditional variance at most $σ^2$. Given initial primal gap at most $Δ$ and dual residual $\|\nabla_y f(x_0,y_0)\|\le G$, the fixed-budget complexity of finding $\|\nablaΦ(\widehat x)\|\leε$ with probability at least $2/3$ is $\widetildeΘ(\sqrtκLΔ/ε^2+κLΔσ^2/ε^4+κ^2σ^2/ε^2+\sqrtκ\log_+(G/(ε\sqrtκ)))$, where $\log_+u=\log\max\{1,u\}$. This characterization holds when $κ$ and $LΔ/ε^2$ exceed universal constants, uniformly over finite dimensions, and the suppressed logarithms are independent of $G$. It establishes the necessity of linear condition-number dependence in the global stochastic cost and identifies a separate statistical refinement cost. A proximal method separates coarse primal progress from one final refinement, while the lower bounds apply to arbitrary adaptive randomized algorithms. Dual initialization contributes only an additive logarithmic cost, yet removing its control eliminates every finite dimension-free complexity bound, even with exact gradients.

Optimization and Control.title: Matching Randomized Bounds for Finite-Sum Nonconvex-Concave Optimization
Optimization and Control.summary: We characterize the randomized component-oracle complexity of finite-sum nonconvex-concave optimization with a bounded dual domain. For $Φ(x)=\max_{y\in Y}n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x,y)$, the goal is to find an $\varepsilon$-stationary point of the Moreau envelope $Φ_{1/(2L)}$ with probability at least $2/3$ and a fixed query budget. Let $A=LΔ/\varepsilon^2$, $B=LD_Y/\varepsilon$, and $\bar B=\max\{1,B\}$, where $Δ$ bounds the initial primal gap and $D_Y$ bounds the dual diameter. For $A$ above a universal constant, the worst-case complexity is \[ \widetildeΘ\!\left(n+A\min\left\{ \sqrt n\,\bar B+\bar B^4,\ n^{3/4}\bar B\right\}\right). \] The bounds agree within constants for $B\le n^{1/4}$ and within one logarithm for larger $B$. Upper bounds require only mean-squared averaged smoothness and concavity of the average in the dual variable; lower bounds already hold under individual smoothness. The lower constructions cover adaptive component selection, arbitrary query norms, private randomization, and outputs that were never queried. A cone construction gives the small-diameter bound, while a serial branch construction and balanced replication give the remaining two regimes. On the upper side, a persistent estimator with primal averaging complements accelerated proximal dual steps equipped with an explicit primal certificate. The characterization takes the worst case over admissible known dual domains and finite dimensions.

Optimization and Control.title: Matching Complexity for Second-Order Stationary Point with Sample Reuse
Optimization and Control.summary: We consider stochastic nonconvex optimization with sample-wise Lipschitz gradients and Hessians, and reusable opaque sample handles. Gradient and complete-Hessian evaluations are charged separately, including both endpoints of a same-sample difference. For fixed positive problem parameters and in the high-dimensional worst case, we prove that the minimax total derivative-query complexity of finding an $(\varepsilon,γ)$-second-order stationary point is \begin{equation*} \widetildeΘ(\varepsilon^{-3}+γ^{-3}). \end{equation*} The upper bound combines curvature-first randomly signed negative-curvature steps with binary-ancestor derivative estimators; a truncated increment estimate charges predictable drift linearly and martingale motion quadratically. The curvature lower bound uses a deterministic smooth bounded-gradient chain, a radial barrier, and a random rotation. The new first-order lower bound is specifically robust to persistent sample reuse and to complete-Hessian access. It uses a slowly parameterized conservative sign chain, a third-order reverse stick-breaking localization inequality, and stateful relative-entropy accounting for reusable handles. Thus the total rate is near-optimally matched for every relation between $\varepsilon$ and $γ$.

Optimization and Control.title: Optimal Feature-Based Newsvendor Policies under Censored Demand
Optimization and Control.summary: We investigate a newsvendor problem where a decision-maker observes a z-dimensional vector of covariates, and wants to learn how much stock to order given a sample of size n of censored demand data to minimize costs. Demand is censored when insufficient stock is available to meet it, and past stocking quantities are known. We propose a new model-agnostic loss function approach to estimate optimal order quantities using observational data, and characterize the optimal newsvendor policy as the policy that minimizes our proposed loss function. Our method requires only a single estimation step, can be scaled to datasets with hundreds of thousands of data points, and does not suffer from the same instabilities as inverse censoring probability weighting methods. We describe how this loss function can be implemented in linear empirical risk minimization, kernel weights optimization and deep neural network algorithms, and provide excess risk generalization bounds for their out-of-sample performance. Moreover, we show through numerical experiments that our method quickly converges to the optimal policy on synthetic data, and leads to improved performance on real world retail data.

Optimization and Control.title: Near-Optimal Exact-Value Zeroth-Order Complexity for Smooth Strongly Convex Optimization
Optimization and Control.summary: We study deterministic adaptive optimization of globally $β$-smooth, $μ$-strongly convex functions using exact scalar function values. Queries and outputs lie in $B_2^d(R)$, and the minimizer lies in $B_2^d(R/2)$. Set $κ=β/μ$, $Q=βR^2/ε$, and $D_d=(d/\log(ed))^{1/3}$. For sufficiently large $d$ and $0<ε\le c_εβR^2$, the minimax value complexity $N_ε$ satisfies \[ \begin{aligned} N_ε&\ge c d\min\{\sqrt Q,\sqrtκ,D_d\},\\ N_ε&\le C d\min\left\{ \sqrt Q,\sqrtκ[1+\log_+(Q/κ)] \right\}, \end{aligned} \] where $c,C,c_ε>0$ are universal constants and $\log_+(t)=\max\{0,\log t\}$. The lower bound uses an exactly shielded smooth chain and batched delayed rotations; the upper bound combines finite differences, acceleration, and restart. When $\min\{Q,κ\}\le D_d^2$, these bounds match up to constants in the accuracy-dominated regime $Q\leκ$ and at constant relative accuracy $ε=Θ(μR^2)$. For arbitrarily higher accuracy in the range $κ\le D_d^2$, the bounds differ by at most $1+\log(μR^2/ε)$; the optimal accuracy dependence remains unresolved in general.

Optimization and Control.title: Near-Optimal Deterministic Exact-Value Complexity for Smooth Convex Optimization
Optimization and Control.summary: We study the deterministic oracle complexity of smooth convex optimization when the algorithm receives only exact function values. The objective is a globally $β$-smooth convex function, all queries and the final output are restricted to the Euclidean ball of radius $R$, and the unique minimizer lies in the ball of radius $R/2$. We establish an upper bound of $O(d\sqrt{βR^2/ε})$ using coordinate finite differences together with an error-robust accelerated projected method. Our main contribution is a matching lower bound, up to the high-accuracy saturation of the construction: any deterministic adaptive value-oracle algorithm requires $Ω\!\left(d\min\{\sqrt{βR^2/ε},(d/\log(ed))^{1/3}\}\right)$ queries. Consequently, the minimax oracle complexity is $Θ(d\sqrt{βR^2/ε})$ throughout the moderate-accuracy regime $βR^2(\log(ed)/d)^{2/3}\leqε\leq cβR^2$ for a universal constant $c>0$. The lower bound must account for the fact that a single exact real value can encode arbitrarily much information. To overcome this difficulty, we construct a single fixed smooth convex hard instance using a Moreau-smoothed biased max chain, an exact prefix-shielding mechanism, and batched delayed rotations. These techniques preserve consistency with the full adaptive transcript and establish the optimality of the square-root complexity branch for deterministic bounded-query algorithms.

Optimization and Control.title: Critical Growth for Stochastic Adaptive Stabilization with an Unknown Input Gain
Optimization and Control.summary: This paper studies adaptive stabilization of a class of scalar discrete-time nonlinear systems with unknown drift coefficients and an unknown nonzero input gain. Under iid Gaussian noise, we establish a necessary and sufficient polynomial criterion for global stabilizability, characterizing the admissible combinations of growth exponents. When the criterion holds, we construct a feedback combining finite calibration with adaptive control. The time average of the squared output converges almost surely to the noise variance, attaining the smallest possible value. If the criterion fails, then for every Borel causal feedback there exist fixed parameter values and an initial state for which the output magnitude diverges with positive probability.

Optimization and Control.title: Matching Higher-Order Oracle Complexity for Smooth Monotone Variational Inequalities
Optimization and Control.summary: We establish near-optimal higher-order oracle bounds for smooth monotone variational inequalities. For fixed $p\ge2$, let $F$ be monotone on a known compact convex set $X$ of diameter at most $D$, with $\operatorname{Lip}(D^{p-1}F)\le L_p$. Each feasible query returns the complete jet $(F,DF,\ldots,D^{p-1}F)$, and the goal is to find $x$ with tangent residual $\operatorname{dist}(0,F(x)+N_X(x))\le\varepsilon$. Writing $Q=L_pD^p/\varepsilon$, we improve the $\widetilde O_p(Q^{1/p})$ upper bound of Chen et al. to $\widetilde O_p(Q^{2/(3p-1)})$ via a dimension-independent deterministic algorithm that returns an explicit tangent-residual certificate. We prove a matching $Ω_p(Q^{2/(3p-1)})$ lower bound for arbitrary adaptive deterministic algorithms and randomized algorithms with per-instance success probability at least $2/3$, without span or tensor-update restrictions. Hence the high-dimensional worst-case oracle complexity is $\widetildeΘ_p((L_pD^p/\varepsilon)^{2/(3p-1)})$. The same method applies to smooth convex--concave minimax problems, improving the fixed-geometry accuracy exponent from $4/(3p+1)$ to $2/(3p-1)$ and matching the known lower-bound exponent.

Optimization and Control.title: Direct Sample-Average Learning for Queueing Control: Gradient-Free Top-$K$ Coarse-to-Fine Optimization
Optimization and Control.summary: We study steady-state queueing control when decisions must be learned from a single persistent operating trajectory: only the implemented action produces data, and the queue is not reset when the action changes. Fixed-event-count cycles yield a direct ratio-of-totals sample-average approximation (SAA) of each action's steady-state cost rate. A Top-K coarse-to-fine search ranks these estimates, retains several promising refinement paths, and concentrates later operation on finer candidate sets, without requiring gradients, convexity, or differentiability. We decompose direct-SAA error into accumulated conditional transient bias and martingale fluctuation. For regenerative queues, a bias-function representation reduces transient effects within contiguous action blocks to boundary terms. Finite-sample stagewise bounds then link estimation accuracy to master-grid identification through guardian retention, and the required queueing and sampling conditions are verified for a persistent-workload M/M/1 implementation. At a common active set, Top-K has a weakly larger guardian margin than Top-1, and an exact-objective example shows Top-1 can discard the optimal refinement branch. Numerical experiments delineate scope rather than universal dominance: Top-K improves terminal identification in the reported LiQUAR and mixed staffing comparisons, while LiQUAR can have lower cumulative learning cost, and GOLiQ is markedly stronger on a smooth benchmark with reliable queueing sensitivities. Direct ranking is therefore best viewed as a complementary method when model-specific gradients are unavailable, inconvenient, or poorly matched to the decision space.

Optimization and Control.title: Three-Body Earth-Moon Transfers with Different Departure/Arrival Orbital Altitudes: New Phenomenon and Diffusion Model-Augmented Construction
Optimization and Control.summary: Construction of Earth-Moon transfers is the basis of missions to explore the Moon and cislunar space. The traditional grid search method suffers from a relatively low convergence rate and computational efficiency, mainly focusing on the distribution of transfer characteristic parameters. Moreover, when constructing transfers with different departure/arrival orbital altitudes, the process of grid search and trajectory correction should be repeated with a low convergence rate and computational efficiency. To address these limitations of the traditional grid search method, this paper is devoted to exploring an effective way to augment the grid search method. Bi-impulsive Earth-Moon transfers from a circular Earth parking orbit to a circular Moon target orbit in the Earth-Moon planar circular restricted three-body problem are considered in this paper. Firstly, the transfers are constructed, and the corresponding solution space is explored in terms of construction parameters, including departure phase angle at the Earth parking orbit, initial-to-circular velocity ratio, and time of flight. An interesting phenomenon about the discontinuous behavior of the time-of-flight distribution with respect to departure phase angle is identified. This phenomenon is further used to train a diffusion model, which aims to augment the traditional grid search method and generate high-quality initial guesses for transfers with different departure/arrival orbital altitudes. The construction results and the preliminary applicable range of the proposed method are presented and analyzed. The proposed diffusion model-augmented grid search method improves the convergence rate by 47.34-56.25$\%$ and saves wall-clock time by 39.39-40.52$\%$ with respect to the traditional grid search method, while ensuring comparable transfer characteristics.

Optimization and Control.title: Thread Scaling of Hexaly on the TDVRPTW across Two Model Encodings. An Experimental Report: Binding Choice, Slice-Count Choice, and Two Thread Ladders
Optimization and Control.summary: Thread scaling in Hexaly on the Time-Dependent Vehicle Routing Problem with Time Windows (TDVRPTW) depends on modeling, and on the language binding through which the model reaches the solver. We compare two encodings, both reaching the solver through its C++ binding: one evaluates continuous travel-time functions exactly through external callbacks, which that binding evaluates concurrently, while the other approximates them with time slices evaluated natively by the solver. Independent CPU accounting confirms that both use the cores they are allocated, but they respond differently to width. The external-function encoding stabilizes, reducing its seed dispersion by about 30% up to 8 threads before widening again, yet its pooled quality barely moves, because nine of the ten instances improve while the hardest one degrades by enough to cancel them. For the time-sliced encoding we first select a discretization on feasibility under the original travel-time functions rather than on approximation error, and the retained setting then improves monotonically with the thread count, gaining about a quarter of its final gap and reducing the seed dispersion by nearly half between 1 and 16 threads. At equal single-threaded budget the two encodings are close, and the small pooled edge of exact evaluation comes from that same hardest instance, so the practical advantage of the discretization is thread scaling rather than fidelity traded for speed. These descriptive results support multi-threading as a way to improve solution quality and stability when the model can exploit it, and they show that binding-level constraints on external evaluation must be measured, not assumed.
Optimization and Control.comment: v3: 22 pages. Corrected author lists in KAYROS, MAMUT-routing and Poryos2026 references. No new experiments or changes to results. Raw experiment data deposited at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22047134

Optimization and Control.title: Anytime Solver Evaluation with a Normalized Signed Primal Integral and Explicit Reference Policies - Extended Version
Optimization and Control.summary: Anytime solvers return usable solutions before they terminate and improve them while time remains. Their progress is commonly summarized by a primal integral, a final gap, or convergence curves. Each summary leaves consequential choices open: how to score a run before its first feasible solution, whether poor incumbents are truncated, and whether the reference value is updated after the experiment or version-frozen beforehand. These choices become visible when runs produce no valid incumbent or improve a published best-known value. We study a normalized signed primal integral built from a bounded relative gap. It assigns an intrinsic worst value to an empty run, requires no acceptance threshold, and assigns negative instantaneous gaps to incumbents that beat a frozen reference. We compare the smooth difference-over-sum kernel with a signed version of Berthold's max-normalized gap and use the former as a working default. We also distinguish analysis-time from version-frozen reference policies and recommend reading the score with the raw final gap, mean convergence curve, and target-attainment curve. We evaluate these choices on a five-arm routing campaign and two model-fidelity ladders. The two signed kernels preserve every panel ordering in this study, whereas a common acceptance threshold compresses the distances between arms and reverses one panel ordering. Updating 54 of the 212 reference values changes score levels and removes all negative scores, while leaving the observed panel orderings unchanged. An exploratory screen also identifies 12 panel comparisons in which similar integral scores conceal materially different endpoints or attainment rates. The implementation, frozen inputs, and generators are openly released.
Optimization and Control.comment: v3: 40 pages, 8 figures, 10 tables. Updated authorship, ORCID identifiers, author declarations and references. No new experiments. Extended version of a manuscript prepared for journal submission. Companion reports: arXiv:2607.23116, arXiv:2608.10079. Data and code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22095718, https://github.com/0nyr/kayros-campaign-analysis

Optimization and Control.title: Constrained modularity maximization in complex networks via branch-and-price
Optimization and Control.summary: Modularity maximization is widely used to identify community structure in complex networks. In many applications, however, community detection must also incorporate prior knowledge and domain-specific requirements beyond network topology. We study constrained modularity maximization with restrictions on the number of communities, must-link and cannot-link relations, and general resource constraints. While fast heuristics can provide high-quality solutions, they generally lack optimality guarantees, whereas exact mathematical-programming approaches can become computationally demanding as the network size and constraint complexity increase. We develop a unified optimization framework offering complementary heuristic and exact solution methods. These include a constrained Louvain heuristic for feasible solution generation, a column-generation heuristic with graph-partitioning-based pricing, and exact branch-and-price algorithms using mixed-integer linear programming and sparse mixed-integer quadratic programming formulations for the pricing subproblem. We develop a cutting-plane procedure providing independent upper bounds to assess solution quality when exact optimization cannot be completed. Experiments on 11 unconstrained networks with up to 1,005 nodes and 30 constrained instances with up to 379 nodes demonstrate the complementary roles of these methods. The column-generation heuristic rapidly improves the constrained Louvain solutions across the tested constraint classes, while branch-and-price using the sparse quadratic formulation solves 29 of the 30 constrained instances to optimality within a one-hour time limit. This formulation becomes particularly effective on larger, sparse, undirected networks by substantially reducing the size of the exact pricing model. Overall, the framework guides method selection to balance computational time, solution quality, and optimality guarantees.

Optimization and Control.title: Beyond Finite-Sum Optimization: A Primal-Dual Method for Decentralized Finite-Max Optimization
Optimization and Control.summary: Many decentralized systems are judged by their worst-performing agents rather than their average performance. We study finite-max optimization over a connected undirected network, where each agent knows only its own smooth, possibly nonconvex objective. Quadratic regularization yields a smooth finite-sum representation with a scalar dual variable and locally computable clipped weights. We develop an alternating primal-dual gradient tracking (APDGT) method, using neighbor communication without any global or centralized projections. Under smoothness and level-boundedness assumptions, a localized Lyapunov analysis with vanishing regularization establishes bounded primal iterates and Clarke stationarity of every accumulation point of their network average. The averaged sequence contains an $\varepsilon$-stationary point, measured by near-active gradients, within $O (\varepsilon^{-3})$ iterations. Synthetic tests and decentralized logistic regression on Fashion-MNIST illustrate convergence behavior and potential improvements in worst-agent performance.

Optimization and Control.title: Strong Consistency, Optimal Tracking and Sharp Rates for the Åström-Wittenmark Self-Tuning Regulator with Unknown Input Gain
Optimization and Control.summary: We study strong consistency and optimal tracking of the Astrom-Wittenmark self-tuning regulator with unknown input gain. Existing results establish consistency of all parameter estimates for the unmodified recursion under additional growth conditions on reference information. Other approaches obtain stability and optimal tracking by adjusting the estimates used in feedback or adding decaying probing signals. For a class of minimum-phase linear systems with martingale difference noise, ordinary least squares (LS) with certainty-equivalent control achieves stability and optimal tracking almost surely for each bounded reference, provided the recursion is well defined. No reference excitation, adjustment of feedback estimates or added probing is required. When at least two parameters are estimated, all parameter estimates are strongly consistent, with squared norm of the estimation error $O(\log\log\log n/\log n)$ almost surely. A law of the iterated logarithm under zero reference shows that this rate cannot in general be improved. We also derive a logarithm law for cumulative squared tracking residuals, with an explicit dependence of the leading term on reference energy. A chi-square limit yields asymptotically exact parameter confidence ellipsoids for each bounded reference. The proof combines a logarithmic lower bound on the cumulative squared difference between an auxiliary LS prediction of the noise and the reference with estimates from the LS recursion. If the gain estimate were inconsistent, these bounds would yield incompatible estimates for the same weighted sum of squares, establishing gain consistency without assuming stability.

Optimization and Control.title: On the Nonoccurrence of Gradient Restart in Nesterov Accelerated Gradient Method
Optimization and Control.summary: Gradient restarting often improves the practical performance of accelerated gradient methods for unconstrained convex optimization problems, but a general theoretical guarantee of such improvement remains unclear. In this paper, we construct smooth, strongly convex objectives with Lipschitz-continuous gradients and corresponding initial points for which gradient restart never occurs, both for Nesterov's accelerated gradient method and for its ordinary differential equation model. From these examples, we conclude that strong convexity and smoothness alone do not guarantee that gradient restart improves the convergence behavior of the accelerated method or its continuous-time model. In particular, for the continuous-time example, the objective gap is asymptotic to $1/(πt^3)$. We therefore obtain a negative answer to the open problem raised by Su, Boyd, and Cand{è}s [\textit{J. Mach. Learn. Res.}, 2016, 17(153), 1--43] of whether gradient restart guarantees linear convergence of the continuous dynamics for smooth strongly convex objectives.

Optimization and Control.title: A Geometric Framework for Stochastic Iterations
Optimization and Control.summary: This paper concerns models and convergence principles for dealing with stochasticity in a wide range of algorithms arising in nonlinear analysis and optimization in Hilbert spaces. It proposes a flexible geometric framework within which existing solution methods can be recast and improved, and new ones can be designed. Almost sure weak, strong, and linear convergence results are established in particular for stochastic fixed point iterations, the stochastic gradient descent method, and stochastic extrapolated parallel algorithms for feasibility problems. In these areas, the proposed algorithms exceed the features and convergence guarantees of the state of the art. Numerical applications to signal and image recovery are provided.

Optimization and Control.title: Sharp Linear Bounds and Exponential Separation for Single-Flip Methods in Absolute Value Equations
Optimization and Control.summary: Rohn's sign-accord algorithm is a classical single-coordinate sign-flip method for $Ax-|x|=b$, selecting the least-index mismatched coordinate at each step. We construct rational instances on which this rule requires exactly $2^{n-1}-1$ flips from natural initialization, even when both $\|A^{-1}\|_1$ and $\|A^{-1}\|_\infty$ are arbitrarily small. We propose two alternative selection rules, Gauss--Southwell and steepest single flipping, which require only one flip on the same instances. A discrete potential framework with positive polarity factors identifies solutions with global maximizers. Under positive polarity with ratio $κ$ and $r=\|A^{-1}\|_\infty<1$, both rules terminate from any initial signature after at most $\lfloor sκ(1+r)/(1-r)\rfloor$ flips, where $s$ is the number of nonzero solution coordinates. For fixed $η_1<1/2$ and $η_2<1$, both rules have worst-case flip complexity $O(n)$ on the class $\|A^{-1}\|_1\leη_1$ and $\|A^{-1}\|_\infty\leη_2$. An $n-1$ lower bound from natural initialization shows that this linear order is sharp. Under stronger, explicit sign-correction conditions, each rule makes exactly as many flips as there are initially incorrect signs among the nonzero solution components. Thus, each rule makes at most \(n\) flips, and this bound is optimal. A five-dimensional example requiring six greedy flips shows that the bound of $n$ does not extend to the entire common small-norm class. Building on Radons--Rump sign certificates, we further develop three classes of sign-flip algorithms using elimination guidance, cyclic scanning, and randomized $m$-flipping. Under $ρ(|A^{-1}|)<1/2$, we prove at most $n$ flips for elimination guidance, $n^2$ inspections for cyclic scanning, and $O(n^2/m)$ expected batch updates for randomized $m$-flipping. Exact computations and retained paired experiments distinguish flip counts from computational cost.

Optimization and Control.title: Distributional Lifting for Discrete Optimization
Optimization and Control.summary: We introduce a framework that transforms discrete optimization into continuous optimization over parameterized probability distributions. The framework reveals a common distributional structure behind several methods that have largely developed independently, including continuous reformulations for multilinear binary optimization, Markov decision processes and reinforcement learning, the cross-entropy method, mean-field variational optimization, and the quantum approximate optimization algorithm. It enables flexible and modular algorithm design, for example, by using neural networks to incorporate contextual information or by enforcing convexity of the lifted problem. We establish two theoretical results: a link between the lifted optimality gap and sampling quality in the original discrete problem, and a convergence guarantee for the lifted optimization problem under suitable conditions. These results lead to a unified algorithmic template based on batched sampling and stochastic gradient updates that is naturally compatible with GPU computation. We demonstrate the framework through three case studies spanning multidimensional knapsack, covering-constrained three-dimensional assignment, and a stochastic mixed-integer location-allocation problem, showing that it can accommodate distinct combinatorial structures and scale to large discrete and mixed-integer settings.

Optimization and Control.title: KAYROS: An Anytime and Exact Solver for the Time-Dependent Vehicle Routing Problem with Time Windows - Extended Version
Optimization and Control.summary: The Time-Dependent Vehicle Routing Problem with Time Windows (TDVRPTW) captures a central difficulty of urban logistics: travel times vary with the time of day, so the cost of a route depends on when it is driven. This paper introduces KAYROS, an open-source solver for the duration-minimization TDVRPTW that is both anytime and exact. It returns improving valid solutions throughout its time budget and can close instances with conditional computational optimality certificates through an integrated branch-price-and-cut component. We extend the composition of continuous arrival-time functions from the literature, previously described only at proof or proposition level, to the left-continuous functions that stepwise benchmarks require. We prove that the composition routine shipped in the checker computes that operation exactly. We analyze when its evaluation and breakpoint normalization are exact in IEEE-754 double-precision arithmetic, and argue that a canonical, epsilon-free checker must define the objective. The anytime layer combines greedy construction, granular time-dependent local search over balanced route trees, and iterated local search, with a fleet-aware descent for a fleet-cost objective. We further propose an anytime evaluation methodology based on a normalized signed primal integral under a pre-committed statistical design. On 212 instances from five families at a one-hour single-threaded budget, KAYROS achieves a pooled anytime score 63.3% lower than the strongest of three available contenders (Timefold, Hexaly, jsprit). All three contrasts are significant under Holm correction. KAYROS improves all 30 high-effort references of Blauth et al. and 10 literature best-known solutions, and publishes 704 such certificates. The solver, benchmarks and campaign data are openly released.

Companion papers and reports: arXiv:2608.18288, arXiv:2607.23116, arXiv:2608.10079. Data and code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22095718, https://github.com/0nyr/kayros-campaign-analysis, https://github.com/0nyr/kayros

Optimization and Control.title: First-Order Primal-Dual Repairs for Scalable Branch and Bound
Optimization and Control.summary: Mixed-integer programs have found applications in many real-world problems but remain difficult to solve at scale. To improve scalability, there has been increasing interest in incorporating first-order methods as subroutines for solving node relaxations, with success primarily on problems involving specific types of constraints. However, when more general constraints are considered, first-order methods cannot be directly applied because, at finite iterations, they typically produce infeasible primal and dual solutions, preventing their direct integration into branch-and-bound. To overcome this limitation, we introduce repair procedures that extract valid primal and dual bounds from infeasible first-order iterates. These bounds enable node pruning, incumbent updates, and early stopping at any iteration. Empirically, our approach achieves one to two orders of magnitude speedups when solving real-world instances (with another order of magnitude speedup when running on GPUs) and certifies optimality on instances that are difficult for commercial solvers.

Optimization and Control.title: On the Linear Convergence of SISTA for Entropic Martingale Optimal Transport
Optimization and Control.summary: We prove a linear convergence rate of a Sinkhorn-type algorithm for entropic martingale optimal transport in arbitrary dimension. The algorithm follows a block-coordinate ascent scheme, alternating exact Sinkhorn updates for the marginal potentials with an explicit gradient step for the potential associated with the martingale constraint. Under irreducibility and non-degeneracy assumptions on the compactly supported marginals, we establish linear convergence of the dual objective values and iterates. Our analysis relies on a pointwise coercivity estimate involving the gradient of the dual functional with respect to the potential for the martingale constraint. This property allows us to establish uniform $L^{\infty}$ bounds on the iterates. Combining these bounds with smoothness and strong convexity modulo affine invariances yields a uniform Polyak--Łojasiewicz inequality along the iterations and, consequently, a linear convergence rate. We complement our theoretical results with numerical experiments illustrating the convergence behavior of the algorithm.

Optimization and Control.title: Risk-averse learning with delayed feedback
Optimization and Control.summary: In real-world scenarios, risk-averse learning is valuable for mitigating potential adverse outcomes. However, the delayed feedback makes it challenging to assess and manage risk effectively. In this paper, we investigate risk-averse learning using Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR) as risk measure, while incorporating feedback with random but bounded delays. We develop two risk-averse learning algorithms that rely on one-point and two-point zeroth-order optimization approaches, respectively. The dynamic regrets of the algorithms are analyzed in terms of the cumulative delay and the number of total samplings. In the absence of delay, the regret bounds match the established bounds of zeroth-order stochastic gradient methods for risk-averse learning. Furthermore, the two-point risk-averse learning outperforms the one-point algorithm by achieving a smaller regret bound. We provide numerical experiments on a dynamic pricing problem to demonstrate the performance of the algorithms.

Optimization and Control.title: KAYROS: An Anytime and Exact Open-Source Solver for Duration-Minimization Time-Dependent Vehicle Routing. A Technical Report and a Case Study in Human-AI Engineering
Optimization and Control.summary: Time-dependent routing recognizes that the same journey can take a different time depending on when it begins. Under duration minimization, even the departure time of each vehicle becomes a decision. Exact methods for this setting exist in the literature, but researchers and practitioners have lacked a ready-to-use open solver that combines rich piecewise-linear travel times, early feasible solutions and optimality claims. KAYROS fills this gap with two modes on one checker-consistent engine: an Iterated Local Search that streams improving solutions and a Branch-Price-and-Cut method that can issue computational optimality certificates under explicit arithmetic and search assumptions. It installs with one command and has no proprietary dependency. The public MAMUT-routing store currently contains 704 KAYROS certificates under a four-solve publication protocol, which has also led to the retraction and repair of invalid earlier claims. The report presents two complementary benchmark contributions to MAMUT-routing. The first integrates Blauth2024, a benchmark from the literature whose travel times derive from measured Uber speeds, for which KAYROS provides new best-known solutions on all 40 instances. The second proposes Poryos2026, a new benchmark of 1,080 paired static and time-dependent instances built from OpenStreetMap road networks and controlled synthetic traffic. Finally, the report describes the intensive human-AI collaboration behind this work and the verification practices that kept its outputs independently verifiable.
Optimization and Control.comment: v4: 31 pages, 7 figures, 4 tables. Updated author ORCID identifiers and software/benchmark reference authorship. No new experiments or changes to results

Optimization and Control.title: Optimal Oracle Complexity of Dual Halpern Iteration in Normed Spaces
Optimization and Control.summary: In this work, we study the convergence and error bounds of dual Halpern iteration for nonexpansive operators in normed spaces. First, we show that dual Halpern iteration exhibits the same optimal residual rate as Halpern iteration in the deterministic setting through a direct convergence analysis. With inexact operator evaluations, we also conduct a convergence analysis in normed spaces and derive the robust error bound of inexact dual Halpern iteration. Based on this robustness result, we study the oracle complexity of stochastic dual Halpern iteration in $(\mathcal{R}^d,\|\cdot\|_p)$ for $p\in(1,\infty]$, using an unbiased stochastic oracle with bounded variance $σ^2$. Notably, for $p\in[2,\infty]$, our method achieves an oracle complexity of $O\left(ε^{-1}+σ^2ε^{-3}\right)$ in its dependence on $ε$ and $σ$, which matches the lower bound for the case $p=\infty$ without a logarithmic gap in the dependence on $ε$.

Optimization and Control.title: A Simple and Unified Method for Gradient-Variation Regret
Optimization and Control.summary: Gradient-variation online learning has attracted increasing attention for its connections to game theory and optimization. It has been studied in both non-stationary online learning, which aims to minimize dynamic regret against time-varying comparator sequences, and universal online learning, which seeks to adapt to unknown loss curvature. Prior work obtained gradient-variation bounds using different techniques tailored to each setting. We propose a simple and unified method based on surrogate losses with a quadratic penalty on decision movement, yielding gradient-variation bounds in both settings. For non-stationary online learning, the method induces an optimistic-to-gradient-variation reduction, enabling a broad class of algorithms to match the rate established by Zhao et al. (2024). For universal online learning, it yields a simple algorithm that matches the optimal universal regret bounds of Yan et al. (2024) while relaxing the extended smoothness assumption. Finally, we apply our method to online games and improve on existing guarantees.

Optimization and Control.title: Scalable Distributed Stochastic Optimization via Bidirectional Compression: Beyond Pessimistic Limits
Optimization and Control.summary: In centralized, distributed, and federated learning with stochastic gradients and $n$ workers, it was recently shown that it is infeasible to find an $\varepsilon$-stationary point faster than $\tildeΩ\left(\min\left\{\frac{d κL Δ}{\varepsilon} + \frac{h L Δ}{\varepsilon} + \frac{h σ^2 L Δ}{n \varepsilon^2},\; \frac{h σ^2 L Δ}{\varepsilon^2} + \frac{h L Δ}{\varepsilon}\right\}\right)$ seconds in both homogeneous and heterogeneous settings under standard assumptions: $L$-smoothness, $σ^2$-bounded unbiased stochastic gradients, and lower boundedness of the function, i.e., $f(x) \geq f^*$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$, where $Δ= f(x^0) - f^*$, $h$ is the computation time, $κ$ is the communication speed between the workers and the server, and $d$ is the dimension of the iterates and gradients. This result is pessimistic since it does not allow a complexity in which both $\frac{d κL Δ}{\varepsilon}$ and $\frac{h σ^2 L Δ}{\varepsilon^2}$ improve with $n$, even when using random sparsification techniques; moreover, this lower bound can be matched by either non-distributed SGD or vanilla Synchronous SGD, which reduces the impact of recent progress in the design of compression-based methods. In this work, we challenge this limitation and propose new compressed methods, Inkheart SGD and M4, and show that under an additional structural assumption, which is necessary due to the lower bound and which does not restrict the class of considered problems, we achieve new state-of-the-art time complexities that break this pessimistic barrier and allow scaling with the number of workers $n$.

Optimization and Control.title: One-Dimensional Symmetry Reductions of the Monge-Ampère Equation on Some Semi-Homogeneous Convex Cones in $\mathbb{R}^4$
Optimization and Control.summary: Motivated by non-symmetric conic optimization, we construct six explicit families of semi-homogeneous proper convex cones $K$ in $\mathbb R^4$. For each family, a specified three-dimensional subgroup of linear automorphisms of $K$ has generic orbits of codimension one. This yields an orbit invariant $t$ and reduces the Monge-Ampère equation $\det F''=e^{2F}$, defining the canonical barrier on $K$, to an ordinary differential equation (ODE) with independent variable $t$. The families include asymmetric power, rotational-power, exponential, and nonabelian-type cones. For the power and exponential cases we derive first integrals and parametric solutions of the ODE. The reductions open the way for computing the canonical barrier on these cones numerically.

Optimization and Control.title: Learning from Historical Transactions: Robust Supplier Pricing and Stocking with Sparse Data
Optimization and Control.summary: Upstream suppliers often set wholesale prices and stocking levels without direct access to detailed end-market demand information, which is instead held by downstream retailers. We study how a supplier can learn from a small number of historical transactions consisting of wholesale prices, retailer-chosen retail prices, and the resulting demand responses. We develop a robust, nonparametric framework that combines inverse optimization with distributionally robust optimization. Historical retailer decisions are used to restrict the set of demand distributions consistent with the observed transactions, after which the supplier optimizes against the least favorable demand response within this ambiguity set. We further accommodate imperfect retailer decisions through two error models (condition error and price error) and derive tractable worst-case response computations based on linear programs and one-dimensional price searches. Numerical experiments across six demand environments show that incorporating historical decision information can generate substantial profit improvements with only a few transactions and that these gains persist under moderate decision errors.

Optimization and Control.title: Simulation-free approximate Bayesian computation for stochastic reaction networks
Optimization and Control.summary: Uncovering stochastic reaction networks from data is central to single-cell biology. Simulation-based inference has evolved into a flexible paradigm for this purpose, circumventing the computational intractability of the likelihood. Notably, approximate Bayesian computation performs this inference by carrying out extensive Gillespie simulations, usually at a high computational cost. Here, we propose a simulation-free approximate Bayesian computation (SFABC) framework that avoids both simulation and explicit likelihood solutions of the network dynamics. Instead, SFABC exploits the Chemical Master Equation to formulate a tractable convex optimization with ensuing constraints, which are then used to accept sampled parameters consistent with the observed data. The resulting posterior approximation comes with theoretical guarantees: it can be tightened systematically, and it provably converges to the exact Bayesian posterior distributions. Using synthetic benchmarks, we show that SFABC matches the accuracy of standard simulation-based algorithms at a substantially reduced computational cost. We then showcase the applicability of SFABC to experimental systems biology by analyzing gene transcription bursting kinetics from snapshot, time-resolved, and cell-cycle-resolved single-cell data.

Optimization and Control.title: Qudit-based scalable quantum algorithm for solving the integer programming problem
Optimization and Control.summary: Integer programming (IP) is an NP-hard combinatorial optimization problem that is widely used to represent a diverse set of real-world problems spanning multiple fields, such as finance, engineering, logistics, and operations research. It is a hard problem to solve using classical algorithms, as its complexity increases with problem size. Most quantum algorithms for solving IP are highly resource-inefficient because they encode integers into qubits. In [1], the issue of resource inefficiency was addressed by mapping integer variables to qudits. However, [1] has limited practical value due to a lack of scalability to multiple qudits to encode larger problems. In this work, by extending upon the ideas of [1], a circuit-based scalable quantum algorithm is presented using multiple interacting qudits for which we show a quantum speed-up for solving the integer programming problem. The quantum algorithm consists of a distillation function that efficiently separates the feasible from the infeasible regions, a phase-amplitude encoding for the cost function, and a quantum phase estimation coupled with a multi-controlled single-qubit rotation for optimization. We prove that our algorithm yields the optimal solution with the maximum measurement probability. The time complexity for the quantum algorithm is shown to be $O(r_P(mn^2log d + d^{n/2}/N_{y_s}^{1/2} + n ε_{\text{QPE}}^{-1}))$ for a problem with the number of variables $n$ taking $d$ integer values, satisfying $m$ constraints with a precision of $ε_{\text{QPE}}$ and $r_P$ repetitions required for reaching a success probability $P$. Compared to the classical time complexity of brute force $O(d^n)$ and the classical exact algorithm $O((\log{n})^{O(n)})$, it incurs a reduction of $\sim d^{n/2}$ in the time complexity (for a polynomial number of repetitions and precision requirements) for solving a general polynomial IP problem.

Optimization and Control.title: ADSWITCH: A Simple First-Order Algorithm for Full-Rank Equality Constrained Optimization
Optimization and Control.summary: A very simple first-order algorithm is proposed for solving nonlinear optimization problems with deterministic nonlinear equality constraints. This algorithm adaptively selects steps in the plane tangent to the constraints or steps that reduce infeasibility, without using a merit function or filter. The tangent steps are based on the AdaGrad method for unconstrained minimization. The objective function is never evaluated by the algorithm, making it suitable for noisy problems. Its worst-case evaluation complexity is analyzed, yielding a global convergence rate in O(1/sqrt{k}), which matches the best known rate of first-order methods for unconstrained problems. Numerical experiments are presented suggesting that the performance of the algorithm is comparable to that of first-order methods for unconstrained problems, and that its reliability is remarkably stable in the presence of noise on the gradient.

Optimization and Control.title: Kurdyka-Łojasiewicz-based convergence analysis with approximate weakly convex subdifferentials: bundle, quadratic penalty, and moving balls approximation methods
Optimization and Control.summary: The Kurdyka-Lojasiewicz (KL) property has been widely used for establishing global sequential convergence and analyzing local convergence rate of optimization algorithms. Most existing analysis frameworks rely on the construction of a suitable KL potential function such that along the sequence generated, it admits sufficient descents and its exact subdifferentials are suitably controlled by successive changes of the iterates. Nevertheless, a handful of important algorithms, such as bundle methods and quadratic penalty methods, are not known to have potential functions verifying the aforementioned properties, rendering their convergence analysis out of the reach of existing KL-based convergence analysis template. In this paper, we develop a new convergence analysis framework to extend the applicability of KL-based analysis. Our framework is built on a weakly convex KL potential function $ψ$. It allows approximate sufficient descents, the use of diminishing stepsizes, and controls on enlarged subdifferentials of $ψ$ known as the $\varrho$-weakly-convex-$\varepsilon$-subdifferentials. We illustrate the usefulness of our framework by establishing the global sequential convergence and analyzing the local convergence rate of some recent variants of bundle method, quadratic penalty method and moving balls approximation method. Specifically, we show that these methods fall under our framework by presenting explicit and natural choices of $ψ$, and derive suitable choices of model parameters, penalty parameters and constraint shrinkage parameters, respectively, for establishing their global sequential convergence and local convergence rate based on the KL property and exponent of $ψ$.

Optimization and Control.title: The resource cost of cooperative invasion
Optimization and Control.summary: A contact network can favor cooperation by sheltering a lineage until its descendants compete with defectors as a group. We determine the contact strengths, invasion times and measurement effort needed to realize this advantage at fixed population size. Individuals reproduce according to averaged cooperation payoffs, and offspring replace neighbors through contacts of equal weight in both directions. Contact contrast is the ratio of strongest to weakest contact. Under weak selection on a six-site path, the least contrast needed to favor a single cooperator over the reverse invasion by a defector grows as $656ε^{-2}$ for uniformly placed mutants and $4050ε^{-3}$ for mutations in newborn offspring, as the benefit-cost ratio $b/c=1+ε$ approaches one. The extra power arises because rare replacement protects a site while suppressing mutation arrival there. Global bounds force two weakly coupled groups and exact mirror symmetry of the least-contrast contacts for sufficiently small $ε$. Under uniform introduction, additional contrast shortens the leading mean time to extinction or fixation in the absence of selection, from $12/ε$ toward $6/ε$ reproduction attempts, and eventually breaks the mirror symmetry of the fastest design. Estimating the uniform-introduction advantage from fixation outcomes of independent completed invasions defines a third optimum. Within the six-site family with mirror-symmetric, strongly separated contacts, we optimize contacts and selection strength with reproduction weighted linearly or exponentially by payoff. At fixed relative precision, with contrast a fixed factor above its minimum, the leading summed trial duration grows as $ε^{-3}$. Efficient measurement accepts a smaller advantage in exchange for shorter trials. The cheapest, fastest and most efficiently measured networks therefore differ.

Optimization and Control.title: Flux-Based Time Bounds for Harmonically Degenerate Quantum Systems
Optimization and Control.summary: We study transfer-time estimates for finite-dimensional bilinear quantum control systems driven by an unbounded scalar control, in both the state-to-state setting (complex projective space) and the unitary synthesis setting (special unitary group). Lower bounds are recalled and refined via spectral and chordal methods. The main contribution is constructive upper bounds: we associate with the system a coupling graph whose edges correspond to non-resonant drift couplings, and construct transfer protocols along spanning trees. In contrast with earlier results requiring full rational independence of the spectrum of the control operator, our estimates allow rational resonances; they incorporate, via explicit correction factors derived from the arithmetic of the spectral gaps, the efficiency of the averaging procedure and of the phase adjustments. As an application, we consider finite-dimensional truncations of the planar quantum rotator under a dipolar electric field, and show that the transfer time between any two modes tends to zero as the truncation dimension grows.

Optimization and Control.title: Hybrid metaheuristics for architectural design optimization under small evaluation and wall-clock budgets
Optimization and Control.summary: Architectural and structural design optimization in parametric software affords about a thousand evaluations of an expensive model for problems with tens of variables, a regime for which most metaheuristics were not designed. On the side of artificial intelligence, two hybrid metaheuristics are proposed: a covariance matrix adaptation evolution strategy (CMA-ES) whose sampling is enriched with differential-evolution trial vectors, and a particle swarm with success-history parameter adaptation, differential-evolution injection and local refinement. A budget-aware delay of population-size reduction in adaptive differential evolution is also proposed. Under a hard cap of 1,200 evaluations, all counted, the CMA-ES hybrid ranks first on seven shifted and rotated functions at 10 and 30 variables and beats CMA-ES on six of seven functions at 30 variables. Ablations attribute this gain to the injection and show that a local search pays off only when its result re-enters the population. The delayed schedule improves three adaptive differential-evolution variants in 40 of 51 comparisons, with no loss. On the side of engineering application, in Grasshopper the CMA-ES hybrid and plain CMA-ES are never significantly worse than the optimizers of Galapagos, SilverEye, Opossum and Tunny on travelling-salesman instances and on a built 85-variable free-form shell, where they end 48 % below the best external tool in 15 minutes. On a 22-variable building-performance problem with binary choices, differential evolution leads instead. Shifting and rotating the functions reverses the rank of Harris hawks optimization. Solvers should therefore be selected by problem structure and stopping time, not by a single ranking.

Optimization and Control.title: The Douglas--Rachford algorithm for normal cones converges only weakly
Optimization and Control.summary: We show that the Douglas--Rachford algorithm applied to two normal cone operators associated with closed convex sets can fail to converge strongly, even when one set is a closed vector subspace, the other is a closed convex cone, and their intersection is a singleton.

Optimization and Control.title: Structural conditions on trust-region radius updates. Part II: second-order convergence and asymptotic radius behaviour
Optimization and Control.summary:
Continuing Part I (arXiv:2606.30202), we ask not which structural conditions on $\{Δ_k\}$ suffice for global convergence but what the radius does; the answers separate the mechanisms by whether the radius is tied to a criticality measure.
  We identify three asymptotic regimes: the criticality-anchored rules give $\sum_k Δ_k^2/M_k < +\infty$, hence $\liminf_k Δ_k = 0$, and $Δ_k \to 0$ once the model Hessians are bounded; the step-driven rules inherit the summability of the step series, hence $\sum_k Δ_k < +\infty$; the fixed-factor rules keep $Δ_k$ bounded away from zero. Near a critical point with positive definite Hessian, convergence of a subsequence forces convergence of the full sequence.
  We then extend the framework to second-order criticality through $τ_k = \max\{\|g_k\|, -λ_k^-\}$, obtaining convergence to second-order critical points with the worst-case complexity $\mathcal{O}(\max\{\varepsilon_g^{-2}\varepsilon_H^{-1}, \varepsilon_H^{-3}\})$, which reduces to $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-3})$ for a common tolerance and is sharp for quadratic models.
  Finally we establish eventual inactivity of the constraint and superlinear convergence, isolating the two properties of the radius rule through which the mechanism enters; the rate itself is mechanism-independent. The criticality-anchored and capped gradient-scaled rules reach inactivity only under a side condition, $ζ> \overlineκ$ or $\overlineμ > \overlineκ$, with $\overlineκ$ a constant of the solution that cannot be checked in advance. These conditions are necessary, not artefacts: on $f(x) = \sin(x)/x$, $\overlineκ$ is unbounded over the minimisers, so no parameter value meets the condition at all of them. Among the rules tied to a criticality measure, only those with an unbounded multiplier escape such a constant.

Optimization and Control.title: A numerical study of radius update rules in trust-region algorithms
Optimization and Control.summary:
Part I [arXiv:2606.30202] and Part II establish which trust-region radius update mechanisms can fail and under which hypotheses they must succeed. Neither says where the thresholds sit once a rule runs with real constants, or how the rule interacts with the model Hessian and the subproblem solver. This paper turns them into nine falsifiable claims and settles what it can, on four designed problems where the theory's quantities are computable and on CUTEst, where only aggregate cost is visible. Every mechanism runs in one Julia package written for this study, so two runs differing in one component differ in nothing else.
  The rule is worth less than the model and more than nothing. Crossing the mechanisms with four model Hessians puts $96.5$ per cent of the variation on the model and $1.6$ on the rule, and the rules separate most under the most accurate model rather than least. Uncapped R-grad is the robust default among the criticality-anchored rules, though the retrospective rule is ahead of it on this collection. No constant escapes the side conditions. For every cap there is a minimiser at which the constraint stays active, and for every anchoring constant a flatness on which escape takes arbitrarily long. The second of these is proved here as well as measured, and the proof uses no property of the model or of the subproblem solution beyond $\|s_k\| \leq Δ_k$.
  The radius rule governs the length of the step, and so the cost of a run. The model decides the search direction, and with it whether the run converges at all.

Optimization and Control.title: On the Peak Estimation of Scalar Polynomial Systems via Integrability
Optimization and Control.summary: We develop a convergent occupation measure framework for peak estimation of scalar polynomial dynamical systems with no a priori state bound. The key observation is that scalar trajectories satisfy a uniform weighted integrability bound whose exponent precisely compensates for the singularity introduced by polynomial compactification. This yields a finite measure formulation with polynomial data. We establish a superposition principle for the resulting weighted continuity equation, prove no relaxation gap and establish convergence of the associated moment-sum-of-squares hierarchy.

Optimization and Control.title: Do We Need Asynchronous SGD? On the Near-Optimality of Synchronous Methods
Optimization and Control.summary: Modern distributed optimization methods mostly rely on traditional synchronous approaches, despite substantial recent progress in asynchronous optimization. We revisit Synchronous SGD and its robust variant, called $m$-Synchronous SGD, which can be interpreted as a method with a backup-worker strategy, and theoretically show that they are nearly optimal in many heterogeneous computation and communication scenarios, which is somewhat unexpected. We analyze the synchronous methods under random times and adversarial partial participation of workers, and prove that their time complexities are optimal in many practical regimes, up to logarithmic factors. While synchronous methods are not universal solutions and there exist tasks where asynchronous methods may be necessary, we show theoretically that they are sufficient for many modern heterogeneous computation and communication scenarios.

Optimization and Control.title: Well-posedness and controllability of hyperbolic boundary control systems on a one-dimensional spatial domain
Optimization and Control.summary: The aim of this paper is to investigate the well-posedness of a class of boundary control and observation systems on a one dimensional spatial domain. We derive a necessary and sufficient condition characterizing the well-posedness of these systems. Furthermore, we show that the well-posedness and full control and observation implies exact controllability and exact observability. The theoretical results are illustrated using Euler-Bernoulli beam models.
Optimization and Control.comment: This work was supported and funded by the European Union (Horizon Europe MSCA project ModConFlex, grant number 101073558) and by the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft (DFG, German Research Foundation) Project-ID 531152215 -- CRC 1701. 25 pages

Optimization and Control.title: Structural conditions on trust-region radius updates. Part I: first-order convergence and complexity
Optimization and Control.summary:
Trust-region methods differ chiefly in how they update the radius, and each rule has traditionally been analysed on its own terms. We show that three structural conditions on the radius sequence suffice: a lower bound relative to the gradient norm, a contraction on unsuccessful iterations, and a controlled expansion on successful ones. A mechanism is weakly admissible if it satisfies the first two, and strongly admissible if it satisfies the first and third.
  Strong admissibility yields the optimal worst-case complexity $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-2})$ for first-order stationarity, and extends global convergence to model Hessians growing linearly with the iteration; weak admissibility gives $\lim_{k\to\infty}\|\nabla f(x_k)\| = 0$ under uniformly bounded model Hessians. Both hold for every rule in the class, so a new mechanism is covered by verifying two inequalities rather than by a fresh convergence proof.
  We verify admissibility for five mechanism classes (fixed-factor, step-driven, retrospective, criticality-anchored and gradient-scaled), prove convergence of the retrospective update under linearly growing model Hessians, and extend the Lyapunov framework of Curtis and Scheinberg (2020), Wang and Yuan (2022) to three distinct scaling factors with decoupled step acceptance, covering $η= 0$; its stochastic version specialises to the deterministic gradient-scaled rule.
  Part II treats the asymptotic behaviour of the radius and convergence to second-order critical points.

Optimization and Control.title: Solving Classes of Linear Programs with Strongly Polynomial Straight Line Complexity in Strongly Polynomial Time
Optimization and Control.summary:
Recently, Allamigeon, Dadush, Loho, Natura, and Végh (ADLNV, SICOMP 2025) introduced an interior point method for linear programs whose number of iterations is bounded by the so-called straight line complexity (SLC) of the instance. This yields a strongly polynomial bound on the number of iterations of the corresponding interior point algorithm for broad classes of linear programs. In particular, in the companion paper we give a strongly polynomial straight line complexity bound for two-variable-per-inequality linear programs. However, in order to obtain a strongly polynomial algorithm for these classes, one also needs to address two important technical issues: initialization and bit-complexity bounds. Standard IPM initialization techniques either require numerical estimates that cannot be obtained in the strongly polynomial model, or involve modifying the instance in ways that do not preserve the geometry of the original LP, potentially affecting the SLC.
  In this work, we present an initialization framework for interior point methods for linear programming, along with a rounding procedure that ensures the continued feasibility of the IPM. We develop a multistage scheme in which each stage can be initialized in strongly polynomial time given the output of the previous stage. Additionally, we address the challenge of controlling the bit complexity of each iterate throughout the algorithm. To this end, we show that it is possible to represent iterates as low-complexity convex combinations of vertices and extreme rays. Our combinatorial rounding step is independent of the algorithm in ADLNV 2025, and can be applied more broadly in the context of path-following methods.
Optimization and Control.comment: This paper is based on the STOC 2024 proceedings paper "A strongly polynomial algorithm for linear programs with at most two nonzero entries per row or column'' , and includes the full details of the initialization framework and the bit complexity arguments

Optimization and Control.title: Attention's forward pass and Frank-Wolfe
Optimization and Control.summary: We study the hardmax limit of self-attention dynamics for token embeddings obtained in the zero-temperature ($β\to+\infty$) regime, and relate it to the finite-$β$ setting. In this limit, the update rule can be viewed as a Frank-Wolfe step for a quadratic objective over the convex hull of the current token embeddings. When the key-query matrix is negative semidefinite, the method linearly contracts all tokens to a single cluster at the origin. When it is positive semidefinite, extending the hardmax rule to the entire convex hull induces a Voronoi diagram: vertices are stationary, interior points remain in their initial cells, and each token moves along a straight line toward its cell's vertex, yielding (super-)exponential convergence. As a byproduct, we also establish well-posedness of the associated ODE limit in this regime. Returning to the finite-$β$ regime, we model self-attention dynamics as a Markov chain and prove dynamic metastability: with high probability, interior tokens reach near-vertex configurations in a constant number of steps and remain within a small neighborhood for times that grow exponentially in the inverse temperature $β$, before ultimately collapsing to the origin. Thus, the hardmax dynamics accurately approximate the finite-$β$ process over exponentially long time horizons.

Optimization and Control.title: Sum-of-Squares Certificates for Copositive Matrices via Recursive Identities: The de Klerk-Pasechnik Conjecture and Hoffman-Pereira Matrices
Optimization and Control.summary: We establish the conjecture by de Klerk and Pasechnik (2002), claiming that the semidefinite bounds $\vartheta^{(r)}(G)(r\geq 0)$ for the stability number $α(G)$ are exact at $r=α(G)-1$, by exhibiting an explicit sum-of-squares certificate. This certificate allows us to recover a known characterization of the minimizers of the Motzkin-Straus formulation for $1/α(G)$. Additionally, we give sum-of-squares copositivity certificates for the matrices satisfying the Hoffman-Pereira sign condition, a crucial condition for characterizing copositive matrices with $\{-1,0,1\}$ entries.

Optimization and Control.title: Single-level reformulations for network pricing under Wardrop equilibrium with separable affine costs
Optimization and Control.summary:
We consider the problem of setting tolls on a subset of the arcs of a congested network so as to maximize the revenue of a network authority, anticipating that users route according to a Wardrop equilibrium. This problem is naturally cast as a bilevel program in which the leader sets tolls while the followers respond by choosing an equilibrium routing.
  We focus on the important special case of separable affine arc cost functions. Under this assumption, Wardrop equilibria admit Beckmann's convex characterization, from which we derive three new single-level reformulations of the bilevel problem, exploiting both Beckmann's formulation and its dual: an arc-based formulation, which we solve exactly, and two path-based formulations, solved by column-and-constraint generation. Beyond the reformulations, we further derive from Beckmann's potential an upper bound on the optimal revenue that can be used to certify optimality gaps across all formulations.
  An extensive computational study on instances derived from the Sioux Falls and Eastern Massachusetts networks compares our formulations with the recent mixed-integer nonlinear formulation of Beck, Labbé and Schmidt. The arc-based formulation solves substantially more instances to proven optimality (within a time limit of 1800 s) than this formulation and, unlike it, returns a feasible solution on every instance. It remains effective on the largest, 74-node network, on which the formulation of Beck et al. solves none. The magnitude of the upper bounds on the tolls proves to be a major driver of tractability: the genuinely hard core of the benchmark emerges once the regulatory cap on tolls is removed. The two path-based formulations, used as heuristics, return a solution within one percent of the optimum on every instance whose optimal value is known, often in seconds where exact formulations reach the time limit.

Optimization and Control.title: Acceleration Survives Heavy Tails and Generalized Smoothness
Optimization and Control.summary: We establish high-probability accelerated convergence guarantees for convex $(L_0,L_1)$-smooth optimization with unbiased stochastic gradients under heavy-tailed noise, assuming a central $α$-th noise moment bounded by $σ^α$, $α\in(1,2]$. Such guarantees are known under classical $L$-smoothness, but extending them through localization over an $O(R)$-radius ball may introduce an $e^{O(L_1R)}$ factor. We avoid this dependence in two ways. First, a two-phase scheme uses Clip-SGD to reach a low-curvature regime, after which clipped stochastic similar triangles (Clip-SSTM) attains, with probability at least $1-δ$, $f(y_K)-f^\star\le\widetilde{\mathcal O}\big(L_0R^2/K^2+σRK^{-(α-1)/α}\big),$ where $R$ bounds the distance from the Phase-II starting point to a minimizer. Second, a modified deterministic weight schedule allows Clip-SSTM to start directly from the initial point, controlling the high-curvature transient before recovering acceleration. With the prescribed initialization, both approaches recover the classical accelerated rate, with $L_1$ confined to an accuracy-independent transient, up to logarithmic factors. The two-phase analysis uses two coupled potentials to preserve the low-curvature regime despite momentum; the one-phase analysis controls the initial high-curvature regime using a modified version of the classical SSTM weight schedule.

Optimization and Control.title: Universal Learning of Nonlinear Dynamics
Optimization and Control.summary: We study the fundamental problem of one-step prediction of a marginally stable unknown nonlinear dynamical system. We describe an algorithm for this problem, based on the technique of spectral filtering, which learns a mapping from past observations to the next based on a spectral representation of the system. Using techniques from online convex optimization, we prove vanishing prediction error for any nonexpansive nonlinear dynamical system with finitely many marginally stable modes, with rates governed by a novel quantitative control-theoretic notion of learnability. The main technical component of our method is a new spectral filtering algorithm for linear dynamical systems, which incorporates past observations and applies to general noisy and marginally stable systems. This generalizes the original spectral filtering algorithm to both asymmetric dynamics as well as incorporating noise correction, and is of independent interest.

Optimization and Control.title: Topological entropy of nonlinear time-varying systems
Optimization and Control.summary: We study the topological entropy of nonlinear time-varying systems. We establish conditions under which entropy is independent of the initial time and derive two general upper bounds based on the matrix measure of the system Jacobian and the spectral abscissa of a Metzler comparison matrix, respectively. A general lower bound is also obtained using the trace of the Jacobian. For interconnected systems, we first derive an upper bound using the matrix measure of an interconnection matrix constructed from the Jacobian blocks. We then establish a new upper bound based on the spectral abscissa of a Metzler comparison matrix, incorporating the interconnection structure through subsystem-wise trajectory-separation analysis. This bound also recovers the two general upper bounds as special cases. All bounds depend on asymptotic properties of the Jacobian over reachable sets or their convex hulls. Simple examples show that either general upper bound may be tighter, while a time-varying Lorenz system illustrates the effects of norm selection and subsystem decomposition.

Optimization and Control.title: Distributed Algorithm for Linear Least Squares Problems via Iteratively Preconditioning by Successive Over-Relaxation
Optimization and Control.summary: This paper focuses on a novel distributed optimization algorithm for solving multi-agent linear least squares problems within a server-agent framework. Distributed methods are particularly suited to large-scale systems. The computational tasks can be partitioned across agents, while local data of one agent remain inaccessible to others. The proposed approach employs an iterative preconditioning scheme with the successive over-relaxation technique, leading to a substantial reduction of the number of iterations required for convergence, which presents a critical advantage where server-agent communication is costly. Theoretical convergence proof of the proposed algorithm is presented. Finally, benchmark problems are tested to demonstrate the performance comparison of the proposed approach over several prominent distributed methods.
